from the desk of

John Keats

John Keats was born in London in 1795 and died at twenty-five. In 1819 he wrote a collection of odes that readers still return to. Two of his greatest odes lie enclosed in the stamps below.

Ode to Nightingale Ode to Autumn

Each one holds an ode. Open it to step inside.

John Keats (1795–1821) was an English Romantic poet whose writing explored beauty, nature, love, mortality, imagination and the fleeting nature of human experience. Despite his short life, Keats became one of the most influential poets of the Romantic era

His odes are especially recognised for their rich sensory imagery, musical language, emotional depth and philosophical questioning. Rather than offering definite answers, Keats allows readers to experience contradictions such as pleasure and pain, beauty and loss, and permanence and change.

Today, Keats's odes are regarded as masterpieces of English literature. Their influence lies in their ability to make readers slow down, observe and imagine

Ode to

Autumn

Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness, Winchester, September 1819

Ode to Autumn

Dear reader, The harvest is in, the light is low, and the day is nearly done. Walk the glade, step into the granary, watch the cider-press, listen at the hive, and gather all 33 lines. Race five minutes of daylight, or put the clock away and wander.

Ode to

Nightingale

My heart aches, and a drowsy numbness pains Hampstead, May 1819

Ode to Nightingale

Dear reader, It is night, and somewhere in the dark a nightingale is singing. You want to follow it, past wine, past weariness, past the edge of what you can see. Walk the poem’s eight stanzas by lantern light, gather all 80 lines, and find out whether the song fades or you wake.
